read.sections.2.text.note: "may" / "probably" became "mungkin" / "kemungkinan besar"; the same pair is used in the simpler text and the self-check. Please check these read as the careful museum-label words intended.
read.sections.2.text.back: A careful historian is honest about uncertainty. The repair shows that someone chose to fix the tin and keep using it. But it does not prove that the owner was poor or careless, because people fix things for all kinds of reasons. Museum labels often use careful words, like "maybe" or "most likely", when the evidence is not yet certain. A good label for this tin might say, "This tin was maybe used to carry the packed lunch of someone who worked at a repair workshop." A dated note, or a list of people who owned this tin, could make this claim stronger.
read.sections.2.text.source: A careful historian is honest about uncertainty. The repair shows that someone chose to fix the tin and keep using it. However, it does not prove that the owner was poor or careless, because people repair things for many reasons. Museum labels often use careful words, such as "may" or "probably", when the evidence is not certain. A good label for the tin might say, "This tin may have carried the lunch of someone who worked at a repair workshop." A dated record, or a list of the tin's past owners, could make this claim stronger.

read.sections.0.text.back: An object that people made or used in the past is called an artefact. When you study an artefact, start with what you can see. An observation is a detail you can notice yourself, with your eyes or hands. The tin has a dent in its lid, the letters "ML" on its side and a hinge that has been repaired. All of these are observations. After that, you can make an inference, that is, an idea you put together from the clues. For example, you might say that the owner used this tin to carry a packed lunch. That could be true, but the tin itself does not tell us.
read.sections.0.text.source: An object that people made or used in the past is called an artefact. When you study an artefact, start with what you can see. An observation is a detail that you can notice for yourself, with your eyes or your hands. The tin has a dent in the lid, the letters "ML" on its side and a repaired hinge. These are all observations. Next, you can make an inference, which is an idea that you build from clues. For example, you might say that the owner used this tin to carry lunch. That could be true, but the tin itself does not tell us.

That could be true. But the tin does not tell us.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Use a second source to test an idea

read.sections.1.text.back: A second source can help you test an inference. The notebook page says that Mina L. put rice and beans into her tin before going to the repair workshop. The tin has the letters "ML", so maybe there is a link between Mina and the tin. This link needs checking, but it does not prove that the tin was hers. The letters could belong to someone else, and objects often move from one person to another. Context can also help. Context is the information around an object, for example the place where the object was found. We know the tin and the notebook were found inside the same box.
read.sections.1.text.source: A second source can help you test an inference. The notebook page says that Mina L. packed rice and beans in her tin before going to a repair workshop. The letters could belong to someone else, and objects often pass from one person to another. Context can help too. Context is the information around an object, such as where it was found. We know the tin and the notebook were found in the same box.

The tin and the notebook were in the same box.

watch.summary.back: This is the same short video as in Lesson 1. The video explains primary sources. A primary source is a thing made or used at the time you are studying. An object can be a primary source, just like a letter or a diary. An object shows what it was made from. An object also shows its marks and signs of repair. Writing shows what its writer saw or did. In this lesson, the tin is one primary source and the notebook is another primary source. If you put the two together, you can build an idea about who used the tin. But finding two objects in the same box does not prove that they had the same owner. So a careful historian says what can be seen, then makes an inference, then names what is still unknown.
